issues.legal_issue: The sufficiency of proof required to establish a will’s genuine execution when circumstances surrounding its making raise suspicion.
material_facts: The testator, who was suffering from cancer, made a will shortly before his death giving his only agricultural land to a niece and excluding his wife and children, including minor children; the reason for this disposition was not established.

The claimed close relationship and care between the testator and the beneficiary were disputed, and the beneficiary did not testify. Her husband, acting as her attorney, gave evidence of an earlier proposed purchase of the land and a substantial advance payment, but no document supported that payment and his evidence about the transaction was inconsistent.

The beneficiary’s husband said that he learned of the will after the testator’s death and obtained the original from the registration office, but how he obtained it was unexplained. The evidence about the will’s preparation and registration raised further doubts, including that registration was said to have occurred beyond office hours; the registering officer did not say that the contents were read over and explained to the testator.

The testator died shortly after the alleged execution of the will, and the land was sold within months of his death. The trial court decreed the suit, but the High Court reversed that decision on the basis that execution had been proved by the attesting witness and registering officer.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was wrong to reverse the trial court’s decision: the circumstances raising grave suspicion about the will were not satisfactorily dispelled, so the trial court’s decree was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, an unprivileged will must be executed in the prescribed manner; under Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, its execution must be proved by at least one available and capable attesting witness. Formal compliance alone does not establish that a will is genuine when suspicious circumstances exist. The propounder bears the burden of proving valid execution, the testator’s understanding and sound disposing capacity, and—if suspicion exists—of removing it with sufficient and cogent evidence. The court must assess the circumstances as a whole rather than begin from suspicion or ignore well-founded suspicion. The Court relied on B. Venkatamuni v. C.J. Ayodhya Ram Singh, Niranjan Umeshchandra Joshi v. Mrudula Jyoti Rao, Rabindra Nath Mukherjee v. Panchanan Banerjee, Venkatachala Iyengar, Madhukar D. Shende v. Tarabai Shedage, Sridevi v. Jayaraja Shetty, and Joseph Antony Lazarus v. A.J. Francis. On the adverse inference from a party’s failure to testify, it relied on Sardar Gurbakhsh Singh v. Gurdial Singh, Martand Pandharinath v. Radhabai, Sri Sudhir Ranjan Paul v. Sri Chhatter Singh Baid, Tulsi v. Chandrika Prasad, and Binapani Paul v. Pratima Ghosh.

predicates.appeal_from_high_court_reversal_in_will_: A civil appeal concerns a High Court reversal of a trial court decision in a suit where the genuineness of a will is disputed.
predicates.grave_suspicious_circumstances_surround_: The evidence shows serious unexplained circumstances about the will’s disposition, preparation, execution, or custody.
predicates.propounder_fails_to_remove_suspicion: The person relying on the will does not provide sufficient and cogent evidence to explain the suspicious circumstances and establish the testator’s informed and freely made execution.
predicates.high_court_relies_on_formal_execution_pr: The High Court reverses the trial court after relying on formal proof of execution without adequately addressing the suspicious circumstances.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns a High Court reversal in a will dispute, grave suspicious circumstances remain unexplained, and the High Court relies on formal execution proof without adequately addressing them, the High Court’s reversal is set aside and the trial court’s decree is restored.
